strengths: The paper addresses two practically relevant and well-motivated questions: when multi-step self-improvement succeeds on a single task, and when easy-to-hard curricula provably outperform fixed-mixture training, in a finite-sample regime that better matches practice than prior continuous-limit analyses.

The theoretical framework is clean and self-consistent: modeling each iteration as MLE on a reward-filtered distribution, with an iterated-map analysis (Corollary 4.4, Theorem 5.2) that yields interpretable levers (task difficulty, budget n, initialization V_p0(θ̂0)), including a phase-transition characterization of the admissible budget (Proposition 5.5, Corollary 5.6).

The proofs are detailed and largely self-contained (Appendices B–C, ~40 pages), with nontrivial technical work, e.g., the conjugacy analysis via Lemma B.2, monotonicity/unimodality results (Lemmas C.1–C.8), and careful handling of finite-sample acceptance counts via Hoeffding's inequality.

The experimental design is thoughtfully controlled: a synthetic shortest-path task with Llama-3.2-1B allows precise control of initialization Pass@1 and difficulty ratios (via CP-SAT-solved dataset partitions), and the observed trends (moderate-difficulty regime, budget phase transition around n≈2000–3000, optimal intermediate β′) qualitatively match the theory; Monte-Carlo simulations directly validate the feasibility/improvement regions.
The work honestly connects predictions to a broader set of empirical findings in the literature (moderate difficulty, larger budgets, saturation), situating the contribution well.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees rely on a finite model class Π with MLE over that class (Theorem 4.1, Lemma B.1). Real self-improvement fine-tunes a continuously parameterized LLM; the defense in Remark 4.2 (tree search over candidate agents, intrinsic dimensionality) is suggestive but the gap between 'selecting one of |Π| candidate models' and gradient-based fine-tuning remains substantial and weakens the direct applicability of the bounds.

The key structural assumptions are strong and not validated: Assumption 4.3 (per-question acceptance rate is at least c·V_p(θ) for all but a γ fraction of questions) and Assumption 5.1 (a power-law separation between adjacent task difficulty ratios, uniform over Θ) are idealizations that are not empirically estimated on the experimental task or on realistic reasoning benchmarks, so it is unclear when the conditions hold in practice.

The comparison between easy-to-hard and the baseline is a comparison of lower bounds (Theorem 5.2(ii)), not of expected rewards. The bounds involve union bounds, Hellinger-based concentration, and the gap term 1−γ, and are likely loose; strictly larger lower bounds do not imply strictly larger actual performance, and the paper's framing ('provably better guarantees') should be interpreted with this caveat, which is not always emphasized.

The improvement condition N(β′,β,ν,V_p0(θ̂0)) < 0 is an extremely long and opaque expression (Definition A.2); while asymptotic interpretations are provided, the practical usability of the criterion as stated is limited.

The empirical validation is confined to a single synthetic graph task (shortest path) with a 1B model and L difficulty levels encoded via l∈{−1,1,2,3}; despite the theory being motivated by mathematical reasoning (DeepSeek-Prover, Goedel-Prover, etc.), no experiments on real math/reasoning benchmarks are provided, limiting evidence that the predicted regimes transfer.

The theory-to-experiment link is qualitative: constants (c, γ, β, β′, ν) are never estimated from data, so the experiments can only confirm directional trends rather than the quantitative predictions (e.g., the Θ((νc−ν)−3) blow-up or the specific threshold values).

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and well-motivated question: when does iterative self-improvement (and easy-to-hard curricula) provably help, in a finite-sample regime rather than the population limit that prior work (e.g., Huang et al.'s sharpening analysis, Sun et al.'s solver-verifier gap) has mostly addressed.

The technical machinery is carried out with care: Theorem 4.1's finite-sample bound via Hellinger concentration on the reward-filtered distribution, the iterated-map view of Corollary 4.4 (identifying an invariant interval of feasible initializations and an inherent saturation ceiling x+(1,nu)), and the feedback-loop interpretation (better models accept more data) are clean and interpretable.

The empirical protocol on the synthetic shortest-path task is unusually controlled: warm-up finetuning to span initial Pass@1 from 6% to 78%, CP-SAT-based partitioning of the training set so that baseline and curriculum partitions satisfy the required per-iteration difficulty constraints, balanced test sets, and 5 seeds per point.

The qualitative predictions (moderate difficulty regime, benefits of larger budgets n and m, saturation below 1, phase-transition in question budget n, moderate adjacent difficulty ratios) are each checked against the synthetic experiments and broadly align with cited empirical findings from real pipelines (STaR, self-taught reasoners, compute-optimal sampling), which supports external validity of the trends.
weaknesses: The guarantees are 'lower bounds on lower bounds': Theorem 5.2 compares bounds derived by chaining one-step concentration inequalities across L iterations, each with a union bound over t, and through an opaque improvement condition N < 0 whose explicit form (Definition A.2) is an enormous, analytically opaque expression. Even when N < 0 holds, no comparison of the actual expected rewards V(theta_E2H) vs V(theta_B) is established, so the headline 'easy-to-hard provably achieves better guarantees' is a claim about bound looseness as much as about learning.

The theory rests on strong and essentially unverifiable assumptions for real LLMs: a finite model class Pi (justified only heuristically in Remark 4.2), Assumption 4.3's per-question coupling alpha(theta,q) >= c*V_p(theta) holding for all but a gamma fraction of questions under every distribution p, and Assumption 5.1's model-invariant power-law separation between adjacent task difficulties with nearly matching upper and lower bounds (beta vs beta'). None of these constants (c, gamma, beta, beta') are ever estimated from the Llama-3.2-1B experiments, so the quantitative predictions (e.g., critical budget nu*) cannot be tested quantitatively.

The experimental validation is confined to a single synthetic graph task (directed shortest path with distances in {-1,1,2,3}) and a 1B model, in a regime where the answer is essentially algorithmically checkable by BFS. There is no evidence the framework transfers to the mathematical-reasoning settings the theory is explicitly motivated by (GSM8K, MATH, theorem proving), where verifier noise, variable-length solutions, and distribution shift would violate the setup.

Novelty is moderate relative to the close prior work the paper itself positions against: Huang et al. (2024) already provides sharpening-based self-improvement guarantees with finite-model-class concentration; Ferbach et al. [5] already analyzes curated self-consuming data optimizing a reward. The main genuinely new element is the curriculum comparison, but it is delivered via the analytically intractable condition N < 0 and Phase-transition characterizations (Proposition 5.5, Corollary 5.6) whose practical content is hard to extract.

Several results are weak in substance: Proposition 4.5 is 'an immediate specialization' of an appendix corollary; Corollary 5.3's interval-length statement is a two-sided O(nu) bound; Figure 4(a)'s empirical gaps are noisy and non-monotone for individual initial Pass@1 values, so the 'first increasing then decreasing' claim about beta' is read off averages rather than robustly demonstrated.

Presentation: the main-text theorems defer their defining conditions entirely to the appendix (footnote 2), so Theorem 5.2 is not self-contained; the notation burden (alpha, alpha^{(m)}, Z, H_t, G, M_i, N, nu*, nu_c, nu_T, nu_0) is heavy, and key claims like 'these sufficient conditions are highly predictive in practice' are supported only by visual inspection of Monte-Carlo plots (Figures 1-2). No code or reproduction artifacts are mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the CP-SAT data-partitioning pipeline and the simulation plots.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question — when iterative self-improvement with verifiable rewards actually works in the finite-sample regime — and frames it through a clean task-centric model (reward-filtered distributions + MLE updates) that closely mirrors practical reject-sampling pipelines (STaR, DeepSeek-Prover, etc.).

The core technical development is substantive and coherent: Theorem 4.1 gives a finite-sample lower bound with an interpretable acceptance-rate feedback loop, Corollary 4.4/Proposition 4.5 convert this into an iterated-map analysis identifying the 'moderate difficulty' invariant interval, and Theorem 5.2 derives explicit feasibility and improvement conditions comparing easy-to-hard curricula against fixed-mixture baselines under equal budget.

The derived qualitative predictions (moderate task difficulty, benefits of larger n and m, saturation below 1, phase transition in the question budget, non-monotonic dependence on adjacent difficulty ratios β′) are falsifiable and are shown to track both Monte-Carlo simulations of the bound and controlled experiments.

The experimental setup (Appendix D) is unusually careful for a theory paper: disjoint warm-up/self-improvement/test splits, class balancing, matched initial Pass@1 across partitions solved via CP-SAT, and 5-seed averaging — giving credible validation that the abstract assumptions (e.g., Assumption 5.1's difficulty ratios) can be instantiated.
Proofs are detailed, largely self-contained, and appear technically correct; the conjugation argument via Lemma B.2 and the geometric-series comparisons in Appendix C are handled with care.
weaknesses: The realizability assumption that the reward-filtered conditional π_{θ⋆_{t+1}} = π_{θ̂_t}·1{s≥τ}/α belongs to a finite model class Π is strong and not convincingly justified; the defenses in Remark 4.2 (finite agent archives, intrinsic dimension) are heuristic. All headline guarantees are population-level statements about a realizable MLE, so the gap between Π and actual LLM fine-tuning limits the reach of the theory.

The comparison result (Theorem 5.2) establishes that easy-to-hard yields a strictly larger lower bound than the baseline — not that it yields strictly better true performance. The paper's practical claims would be strengthened by discussing when these lower bounds are tight; as written, the 'provably better' framing slightly overstates what is proven.

Key assumptions are heavy and hard to verify in practice: Assumption 4.3 (α ≥ c·V_p for all but a γ-fraction of questions), the power-law difficulty separation in Assumption 5.1, and the conditions {M_i < 0}, N < 0, which involve constants (c, γ, c_δ) that a practitioner cannot estimate; the paper acknowledges feasibility is a 'useful proxy' but the constants may make the conditions vacuous in realistic settings.

Empirical validation is limited to a single synthetic task (shortest-path on small graphs) with a 1B model, while the motivation and related work emphasize mathematical reasoning; there is no experiment on any real benchmark (e.g., GSM8K/MATH), so external validity remains untested. Figures 1–2 validate consistency of the theory with itself (Monte-Carlo of the maps) rather than the modeling assumptions.

Presentation: the improvement condition N < 0 (Definition A.2) is an opaque multi-line expression deferred to the appendix, making the central Section 5 result difficult to interpret; the main text would benefit from a structural interpretation of N before the raw formula. There are minor writing defects (e.g., 'Theorem 4.1 highlight', punctuation errors in Lemma C.2's proof).

Reproducibility of the empirical part is decent in the appendix, but no code release is stated, and several experimental choices (warm-up configurations used to hit target initial Pass@1 values) are only partially specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: a finite-sample, task-centric theory of iterative self-improvement (STaR-style reject-sampling + MLE) and of easy-to-hard curricula, going beyond prior continuous-limit analyses (sharpening, solver-verifier gap).

The core technical development is clean and appears correct: Theorem 4.1 gives a one-step expected-reward lower bound via Hellinger-distance uniform bounds over a finite model class; the multi-step analysis (Corollary 4.4, Proposition 4.5) reduces dynamics to an iterated one-dimensional map F whose fixed-point structure is analyzed exactly via the cubic x(1-x)^2 = sigma^2 (Lemma B.2, Corollary B.3). Full proofs are provided in the appendix and are detailed and self-contained.

The qualitative insights are well-motivated and practically relevant: a finite-sample feedback loop (better models accept more data), an inherent upper bound below 1-gamma explaining saturation, a 'moderate difficulty' invariant interval I(1,nu), and a phase transition in the sample budget for curriculum advantage (Proposition 5.5, Corollary 5.6).

Experiments span a synthetic shortest-path task with controllable difficulty and budgets, plus GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics across six base models; observed trends (moderate-difficulty regime, saturation, budget effects, unimodal dependence on difficulty ratio beta') are consistent with the theory, and the methodology for controlling initial Pass@1 (CP-SAT data selection) is thoughtful.

The writing is generally clear, the notation table and deferred definitions (Appendix A) help readability, and the Monte-Carlo figures connecting the sufficient conditions {M_i<0}, N<0 to actual dynamics are a useful addition.
weaknesses: The theory rests on strong idealizations: a finite model class with exact realizability (the population filtered conditional p'_{theta_t} belongs to Pi), and Assumption 4.3 (per-question acceptance rate alpha(theta,q) >= c*V_p(theta) for all but a gamma fraction of questions). Both are essentially assumed rather than derived, and realizability is particularly strong: the proof exploits that the population MLE exactly matches the filtered conditional. Real LoRA/SGD fine-tuning deviates substantially from the idealized one-shot population MLE, and the paper does not quantify this gap.

The theoretical results are lower-bound-only statements. The feasibility and improvement conditions (M_i < 0, N < 0, Definition A.2) characterize when the lower bound is monotone/tighter, not the actual dynamics; the improvement condition N is an extremely complicated sufficient condition derived via a nu=0 perturbation argument, and its tightness/predictive value beyond matching qualitative trends is not established.

Empirical validation is largely qualitative. No experiment compares the predicted quantitative lower bound trajectory {F^t(V)} to observed rewards, or estimates the constants (c, gamma, c_delta, c_delta') on real tasks. Some benchmark results (e.g., several rows in Table 4 with gaps within or below one standard error, such as nearest_integer_root and place_value) are consistent with noise, and seed counts / significance testing for the benchmark experiments are not fully reported.

The power-law difficulty separation (Assumption 5.1) is a somewhat ad hoc modeling choice; the benchmark curriculum experiments use a relaxed rho-interpolation matrix W=(1-rho)U+rhoI rather than the clean staged curriculum analyzed in Theorem 5.2, weakening the theory-experiment correspondence for the main curriculum theorem.

Multi-step probability handling is informal: guarantees across t iterations are union-bounded (probability 1 - t(delta+delta')), and the treatment of the random number of accepted samples n_t^(m) as conditioning for the i.i.d. application of Lemma B.1 glosses over the dependence between n_t and the accepted data; w.h.p. statements are used without explicit probability bookkeeping.

Reproducibility is moderate: hyperparameters and dataset construction are described, but no code release or repository is mentioned, and several experimental details (e.g., number of seeds for benchmark tables, verifier implementation, acceptance threshold choices) are incomplete.
There is no explicit limitations section discussing the gap between the idealized update rule and practical fine-tuning, or the scope of the assumptions.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and theoretically under-specified question: when does finite-sample iterative self-improvement work, and when does easy-to-hard scheduling provably help. The finite-sample regime is a genuinely relevant angle, since infinite-sample analyses (e.g., sharpening, solver-verifier gap views) predict implausible conclusions such as guaranteed performance above the threshold after a single iteration.

The theoretical development is substantial and largely self-contained: Theorem 4.1 gives a clean single-step finite-sample lower bound with the interpretable acceptance-rate feedback loop; Corollary 4.4 composes it into a multi-step iterated map F; Theorem 5.2 provides explicit feasibility ({M_i < 0}) and improvement (N < 0) conditions for the curriculum comparison, with a full proof chain in the appendix (including careful asymptotics in Lemmas C.1–C.9).

The empirical program is reasonably thorough and well-matched to the theory: a synthetic shortest-path task allows direct control of V_p(θ0), n, m, and difficulty ratios; Monte-Carlo simulations visualize the feasibility/improvement regions; and experiments span six base models on GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics. Trends such as moderate-difficulty optimality, budget effects, and the phase transition in n are qualitatively consistent with the derived conditions (Figures 1–4, Tables 1–4).

Experimental details are unusually complete for a theory paper: dataset construction, CP-SAT-based data selection to enforce controlled partitions, LoRA hyperparameters, seeds, and test-set balancing are all documented in Appendix D, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The gap between the theory and the claims is larger than acknowledged. All curriculum conclusions compare lower bounds (G∘H∘...∘H vs F^L), not actual performance. A strictly larger lower bound for easy-to-hard does not imply better actual final performance, yet the abstract and introduction present curricula as 'provably better guarantees' and the experiments as validating 'better guarantees than training on fixed mixtures.' The empirical gains in Table 4 are noisy (some modules show negative gaps at several ρ values), and the qualitative 'first increasing then decreasing' trend is only loosely matched to the derived conditions.

The assumptions are strong and largely unverified. Assumption 4.3 (α(θ,q) ≥ c·V_p(θ) for all but a γ fraction of questions) and Assumption 5.1 (model-invariant power-law difficulty separation for all θ in a neighborhood Θ) must hold throughout the entire training trajectory, but the empirical validation of β/β' (Figure 5) is computed only at the initialization model. There is no direct empirical check of Assumption 4.3 on any benchmark.

The finite model class Π assumption is questionable for LLM fine-tuning. The justification via tree-search over candidate agents and intrinsic-dimension arguments (Remark 4.2) is indirect. Moreover, the actual update is LoRA fine-tuning for one epoch on a random number of accepted samples, which deviates substantially from the idealized empirical MLE over Π; the paper does not analyze this discrepancy.

The benchmark experiments are weak evidence for the central claims. On DeepMind Mathematics (Table 2), initial accuracies are 74–98%, so the 'self-improvement' setting is nearly saturated; Qwen3-32B degrades, and Llama gains (~17 points) appear on an artificially easy module selection. On GSM8K, improvements are 2–5 points and two models get worse. The 'easy-to-hard' partition on GSM8K is constructed by matching initial performance across rounds rather than by genuine difficulty, which weakens the link between the curriculum experiments and the theory's difficulty-separation assumption.

The improvement condition N < 0 (Definition A.2) is an opaque, lengthy expression; the paper's claim that the sufficient conditions are 'highly predictive in practice' rests mainly on eyeballing Monte-Carlo trends (Figures 1–2) rather than quantitative prediction, e.g., predicting the observed transition window n ∈ [2000, 3000] from the theory.

The multi-step analysis quietly changes the setting: Theorem 4.1 requires ess inf α > 0 and Assumption 4.3 requires θ to stay in a small neighborhood of initialization, but there is no analysis of whether iterated updates remain in Θ. The probability bound degrades as 1 − t(δ+δ'), which is fine but limits practical t.

No explicit limitations section; the conclusion does not discuss the restrictive assumptions, the bound-vs-performance gap, or the synthetic-task-only control of difficulty. Code release is not mentioned.

strengths: The paper addresses two practically relevant and well-posed questions: when multi-step self-improvement happens on a single task, and when easy-to-hard scheduling provably improves over fixed-mixture training, and it answers both within a coherent task-centric framework (Sections 3-5).

The finite-sample perspective is genuinely valuable: Theorem 4.1 and the iterated-map view (Corollary 4.4, Proposition 4.5) explain phenomena that population-level analyses miss, including the feedback loop (better models accept more data), moderate-difficulty requirement, saturation, and the role of budgets n and m.

The curriculum analysis (Theorem 5.2, Corollaries 5.3 and 5.6) yields concrete, interpretable predictions: moderate adjacent difficulty ratios, a critical sample budget with a sharp phase transition, and initialization constraints; the remarks connect the abstract conditions to actionable guidance.

Empirical validation is unusually thorough for a theory paper: a synthetic shortest-path task with precise control over initialization reward, budgets, and difficulty ratios; Monte-Carlo checks of the feasibility/improvement regions; and consistent trends on GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics across six base models (Tables 1-4), including use of the dataset's native difficulty partition.

The appendix contains detailed proofs (conjugacy argument for F(x) = 1 - gamma - sigma/sqrt(x), geometric-sum arguments, implicit-function-theorem-based monotonicity analysis), and experimental setup is documented with hyperparameters, prompt templates, and data-construction procedures supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The assumptions are strong and hard to verify in practice: a finite model class Pi containing the reward-filtered conditional distribution, the reward-acceptance coupling in Assumption 4.3 (with constant c and small gamma holding over a neighborhood Theta for all distributions p), and especially the power-law, model-invariant difficulty separation in Assumption 5.1. The practical plausibility of Assumption 5.1 for real LLMs and task families is asserted rather than demonstrated, so the generality of the curriculum conclusions is unclear.

The central comparison in Theorem 5.2 is between lower bounds, not between actual expected rewards; a strictly larger easy-to-hard lower bound does not establish that the curriculum actually outperforms the baseline. The abstract's phrasing ('provably achieve better guarantees') is careful, but the gap between bound-tightness and true performance is never quantified.

Several steps in the more involved appendix proofs appear loose or sketchy rather than fully rigorous. Examples include Lemma C.1's monotonicity argument (relegated to 'comparison statements' whose verification is partly informal), Lemma C.2's Puiseux-expansion matching argument (the dominant Theta(1) contribution is left ambiguous between T2 and T3, and the conclusion is only claimed up to order nu^2), and the claim in the proof of Theorem 5.2 that the chained iterates stay within the invariant intervals, which is asserted rather than carefully proved. These affect confidence in Corollaries 5.5-5.6.

The improvement condition N < 0 (Definition A.2) is an opaque multi-line expression; despite Remarks 5.7.1-5.7.4, its direct interpretability and checkability in practice are limited, and the feasibility/improvement dichotomy is derived only for this specific sufficient condition.

The theory-empirics connection is qualitative: experiments validate trends (moderate difficulty, larger budgets, interior rho), but no quantitative comparison of the predicted bounds against measured performance is provided, and the modeled procedure (population MLE over a finite class) departs substantially from the actual LoRA fine-tuning used.

Table 4 results are noisy with several negative gaps and large standard errors, and the exclusion of modules with beta' < 0.1 or gap variation below 1% introduces a selection criterion that could bias the reported curriculum benefit toward the paper's predictions.

Presentation is dense: the key conditions {M_i} and N are deferred to the appendix, notation is heavy, and the main theorem statements are difficult to parse without constant reference to Definition A.1/A.2; no explicit statement about code release is included.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question — when does iterative self-improvement of LLMs provably work in a finite-sample regime — and develops a clean task-centric framework (MLE on reward-filtered distributions) that closely mirrors practical generate-and-filter pipelines.

The theoretical development is substantial and technically careful: Theorem 4.1 gives finite-sample single-step guarantees with an explicit effective-sample-size effect (feedback loop between model quality and accepted data volume), Corollary 4.4/Proposition 4.5 yield an iterated-map analysis revealing the moderate-difficulty regime and inherent upper bound, and Theorem 5.2 provides concrete feasibility ({M_i<0}) and improvement (N<0) conditions under which easy-to-hard curricula strictly beat fixed-mixture training. The proofs in Appendices B–C are detailed and largely self-contained, including careful asymptotic analysis (Lemmas C.1–C.11) of the phase transition in the sample budget.

Validation is multi-layered: Monte-Carlo simulations directly visualize the lower-bound dynamics, a synthetic shortest-path task allows precise control of initialization reward, budgets, and difficulty ratios, and standard benchmarks (GSM8K, DeepMind Mathematics across multiple base models) exhibit trends consistent with the theory (moderate difficulty, budget effects, interior optimum in difficulty ratio, saturation). The use of the dataset's native easy/medium/hard split and the rho-interpolation design is sensible.

Transparency and honest treatment of limitations: the paper discusses clean-reward assumptions, noisy-reward extensions, and connections to test-time training in Appendix E; notation is well documented (Table 5), and the baseline/curriculum comparison is defined precisely.
weaknesses: The modeling assumptions are stylized: the finite model class Π assumption (with the filtered conditional assumed to lie in Π) is strong, and its justification via the Huxley-Goedel machine and intrinsic-dimension arguments (Remark 4.2) is heuristic. Similarly, Assumption 4.3 (per-question acceptance rate bounded below by c*V except on a gamma-fraction of questions) and the power-law difficulty separation in Assumption 5.1 are strong structural constraints whose realism is only partially supported empirically.

The central curriculum result (Theorem 5.2(ii)) is a comparison of lower bounds, not of actual expected rewards, so the 'easy-to-hard is provably better' claim is strictly about guarantee tightness; the gap between the theory's bound comparison and real performance is acknowledged implicitly but not quantified.

Empirical validation is largely qualitative/trend-level. The claimed 'highly predictive' conditions are checked by matching directional trends (e.g., interior optimum in beta', budget clustering between 2000-3000), not by fitting or quantitatively testing the bounds; Table 4 shows considerable noise and negative gaps in several modules, and the module-exclusion rule (beta' < 0.1 or gap variation < 1%) introduces some selection.

The experimental pipeline (LoRA fine-tuning with SGD) departs from the idealized population/empirical MLE analysis, and no experiments test the multi-candidate (m>1) part of Theorem 4.1 on standard benchmarks beyond the synthetic setting; constant-level tightness of the bounds is not assessed.

Some presentation issues: the improvement condition N and feasibility conditions M_i are only defined in a dense appendix (Definition A.2) and are hard to parse; the results would benefit from cleaner statements of the main sufficient conditions in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant question: providing finite-sample theoretical grounding for iterative self-improvement via reject sampling, which prior theory (e.g., sharpening or solver-verifier gap views) analyzes only at the population/continuous limit.

The core technical development is coherent: Theorem 4.1 gives a clean single-step lower bound revealing a feedback loop between model quality and effective sample size, and Corollary 4.4/Proposition 4.5 package multi-step dynamics into an interpretable iterated map F with an invariant interval.

The comparison between easy-to-hard curricula and fixed-mixture baselines (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3, 5.6) is a genuinely under-explored angle, and the identification of 'moderate difficulty separation' and a critical sample budget gives testable qualitative predictions.

The empirical validation is broad: a controllable synthetic shortest-path task, Monte-Carlo simulations of the bound dynamics, and experiments on GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics across six base models, with overall trends consistent with the qualitative predictions (moderate difficulty, budget effects, saturation, phase transition in n).
The proofs are detailed and appear careful (e.g., the conjugacy argument in Corollary B.3, the Puiseux-expansion analysis in Lemma C.2/C.3).
weaknesses: The key modeling assumptions are strong and arguably unrealistic for the claimed setting: (i) a finite model class Π with the requirement that the population optimizer of each iteration lies in Π (a per-step realizability assumption that essentially hard-codes the conclusion); (ii) Assumption 4.3 coupling per-question acceptance to expected reward with an unknown exception fraction γ; and (iii) Assumption 5.1 requiring a model-invariant power-law difficulty ordering within Θ. The justifications offered (Remark 4.2) are heuristic. Without these, the bounds could be vacuous (e.g., the ess inf α > 0 requirement in Theorem 4.1 can be arbitrarily small).

The central results are lower bounds on lower bounds: the improvement condition N < 0 guarantees only that the easy-to-hard lower bound exceeds the baseline lower bound, not that actual performance improves. The gap between these bound-level statements and the empirical Pass@1 comparisons is not quantified anywhere.

The improvement condition N is an opaque, page-length expression (Definition A.2) with unknown constants (c, γ, β, β′, δ, δ′); in practice the conditions cannot be checked or used for scheduling decisions, limiting the theory's actionable value beyond qualitative trends.

The experimental support for the curriculum claims is the weakest part of the paper: Table 4 shows several negative gaps and large standard errors, and modules are excluded post hoc (β′ < 0.1 or gap variation < 1%), raising selection concerns. Many effects are a few percentage points with overlapping error bars, and the agreement with theory is only qualitative ('consistent with Remark X'), with no calibration of predicted vs. measured thresholds (e.g., the predicted critical n for the phase transition is never quantitatively compared).

The insights, while correct, are largely expected: larger budgets and moderate difficulty help self-improvement, and curricula help when difficulty levels are not too separated — these echo known empirical findings the paper itself cites ([28], [29], [2, 41, 43]). The novel quantitative content lives inside conditions that are hard to interpret, so the originality is moderate.

The theory assumes exact empirical MLE over the accepted set with i.i.d. accepted samples, while the experiments use LoRA fine-tuning, learning-rate constraints, and minimum-step floors; the mismatch is acknowledged nowhere in the main text, and no ablation isolates whether the observed trends are driven by the mechanism the theory identifies (e.g., acceptance-rate feedback) rather than generic fine-tuning dynamics.

Presentation of the theoretical core is heavy: the multi-condition feasibility set {Mi < 0}, the map definitions, and the phase-transition statements (Proposition 5.5, Corollary C.4) require substantial effort to parse, and the 'informal vs. formal' split adds friction without compensating clarity.

Reproducibility is adequate in structure (hyperparameters, prompts, dataset construction are given), but the CP-SAT-based data selection procedure and warm-up initialization procedure are described too loosely to be reliably reimplemented, and no code release is stated.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and under-theorized question: when does multi-step self-improvement with reward-filtered self-generated data provably work, and when does easy-to-hard task scheduling beat a fixed mixture? This task-centric framing is a sensible and useful complement to prior model-evolution theories (e.g., sharpening, solver-verifier gap views).

The finite-sample analysis (Theorem 4.1) is well motivated: it correctly identifies that population-level analyses would misleadingly guarantee V >= tau after one iteration, and the derived bound captures the feedback loop where stronger models accept more data (Z/a ratio decreasing in m, effective sample size growth), explaining both sustained improvement and saturation.

The multi-step characterization via the iterated map F (Corollary 4.4, Proposition 4.5) yields interpretable takeaways: moderate task difficulty, larger budgets enlarging the admissible initialization interval, and an inherent upper bound below 1-gamma that rationalizes follow-up RL phases.

The curriculum analysis (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3, 5.6, Remarks 5.7.x) produces non-obvious, testable predictions: a critical sample budget with sharp phase-transition behavior, moderate adjacent-difficulty ratios being optimal, and a feasibility/improvement dichotomy as the budget varies.

Experimental validation is layered: Monte-Carlo simulations directly visualize the feasibility/improvement intervals (Figures 1-2), a synthetic shortest-path task gives controlled tests of the difficulty-ratio and budget predictions (Figures 3-4), and standard benchmarks (GSM8K, DeepMind Mathematics with native easy/medium/hard splits) show consistent qualitative trends (Tables 1-4), including agreement with the interior-optimum difficulty-ratio prediction.

Reproducibility is strong: prompt templates, dataset construction (CP-SAT-based data selection), hyperparameter tables, split details, and run averaging over seeds are all documented; the Appendix E discussion of reward noise and test-time-training extensions is an honest scoping of limitations rather than overselling.
weaknesses: The modeling assumptions are strong and somewhat ad hoc. Assumption 4.3 posits a global, model-independent coupling constant c with a small exceptional-mass gamma, and Assumption 5.1 imposes a power-law separation between adjacent task difficulties that must hold uniformly over a model neighborhood; the entire curriculum analysis rests on these, and neither is verified on the real benchmarks used.

All guarantees are one-sided lower bounds on the reward trajectory of an idealized population MLE within a finite model class II. As such, they establish feasibility of improvement but say little about whether the actual update improves, and the empirical MLE over LoRA-finetuned LLMs differs substantially from the idealized estimator (one epoch, no exact MLE, misspecified model class).

The key improvement condition N < 0 (Definition A.2) is an extremely complicated closed-form expression, and feasibility conditions {M_i < 0} are likewise opaque; the paper acknowledges these serve as proxies validated only via Monte-Carlo simulation, which limits their practical usability as design criteria.

Much of the mathematical content reduces to the analysis of a scalar recursion F(x) = 1 - gamma - c_S nu/(c sqrt(x) - c_S nu); the per-iteration statistical content is a single concentration inequality (Lemma B.1), so the technical depth is moderate relative to the length of the analysis (the lengthy Puiseux expansions in Lemmas C.2-C.8 are delicate but of limited conceptual import).

Empirical support on standard benchmarks is largely qualitative: results are described as 'consistent with' the theory, but the theory's constants (c, gamma, nu*) are never estimated or checked; several results are also negative (Llama models degrade on GSM8K, Qwen3-32B degrades on DeepMind Mathematics), and Table 4 excludes modules with small effects or gap variation under 1%, which raises a selection concern for the curriculum comparison.

The number of self-improvement iterations analyzed/evaluated is small (L = 3-4), and the theorem compares lower-bound sequences rather than actual performance, so the claimed superiority of easy-to-hard scheduling (part ii of Theorem 5.2) is verified empirically only in aggregate trend (Figure 4, Table 4) with mixed per-module results (e.g., negative gaps at larger rho for several modules).
